## Introduction

Large language models can call tools: given a user's request and a list of functions, they write the
calls that answer it. Small models do this cheaply, and can run where a large one can't, but they do
it worse. The usual fix is to fine-tune the small model on examples of the task. That needs answers,
and good answers are expensive.

Often, though, a better model is at hand. **Distillation** trains a small model, the *student*, to
imitate a larger one, the *teacher*. The teacher can answer every query we have, so the student can
learn without a single human-written label. The question is how much of the teacher's skill
survives the trip, and which way of passing it on works best.

This essay follows one such attempt from start to finish. The teacher is Qwen3.5-2B, the student
Qwen3.5-0.8B, from the same family and with the same tokenizer. The task is single-turn function
calling, the data is Salesforce's xLAM-60k, and everything runs on one RTX 3060 with 12 GB. The
question is:

> **Without labels, how close does the student get to one trained on gold answers, per GPU-hour?**

Every method below is labelled by whether its training reads gold. The label-free ones answer the
question; the ones with labels are the reference for what labels buy.

::: {.column-margin}
Why this pair and this question: [ADR 0004](decisions/0004-student-teacher-pair.html),
[ADR 0007](decisions/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.html). Thinking mode is off for both
models ([ADR 0003](decisions/0003-thinking-off.html)).
:::

## The data

[xLAM-60k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k) holds 60,000 tasks
like this one, each a user query, the tools on offer and the gold answer:

```{=html}
<div class="task"><div><span class="k">Query</span>Give me the forecast for Lisbon.</div><div><span class="k">Tools</span>get_forecast(city: str, days: int, optional, default 7), get_time(city: str), …</div><div><span class="k">Answer</span>[{"name": "get_forecast", "arguments": {"city": "Lisbon", "days": 3}}]</div></div>
```

The model reads the tools and the query through Qwen's chat template and must answer with the JSON
list and nothing around it. Answers range from one call to several calls to different tools.

We split the data into `{python} n(splits["train"])` rows for training,
`{python} n(splits["validation"])` for validation and `{python} n(splits["test"])` for test. xLAM
asks the same sentence many times with different values ("the factorial of 7", "of 10"), so rows
are grouped by their query and whole groups go to one split: no query appears in two. Exact
duplicates were collapsed before splitting; contradictory answers, code written in place of a value
and answers repeated from validation or test were then removed from train only. Checkpoints and settings are chosen on validation; test is run once, for the numbers reported.

::: {.column-margin}
Every finding about the data and what was done about it:
[the dataset card]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/DATASET.md). The split:
[ADR 0001](decisions/0001-train-validation-test-split.html).
:::

### When the gold answer is the problem

Before any training, the baselines' mistakes looked suspicious. Models of 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters
made about the same number of wrong-argument errors, and errors that don't shrink with a model five
times larger point at the answers, not the models. Is "3% interest" `3` or `0.03`?

So we audited the test rows the baselines got wrong, `{python} n(len(audit))` of the
`{python} n(splits["test"])`, asking one question: *would a careful person, reading only the query
and the tool specs, write this gold answer?* The labelling was blind to which model erred.

| Verdict | Rows |
|:---|---:|
| Sound: what a careful person would write | `{python} n(sum(r["verdict"] == "label_sound" for r in audit))` |
| Ambiguous: one reasonable answer among several | `{python} n(verdicts["label_ambiguous"])` |
| Wrong: contradicts the query or specs, or makes a value up | `{python} n(verdicts["label_wrong"])` |

: The label audit, over the test rows any baseline got wrong. {#tbl-audit}

::: {#fig-gold-wrong}

```{python}
example("gold-wrong")
```

A gold label the audit found wrong (the shortest such test row where B disagrees with gold). Every
model here is wrong, and the marks show differences from a gold the audit found wrong: strict exact
against it would also mark a right answer wrong.
Rows like this are why methods are compared on test-clean.
:::

**test-clean** is test without the ambiguous and wrong rows, `{python} n(splits["test-clean"])`
rows, and it is where methods are compared. On raw test, a method can gain by learning gold's
quirks, such as which of two reasonable answers xLAM happened to choose. Test's labels themselves are
never edited, so numbers on raw test stay comparable with other work.

::: {.column-margin}
The rubric: [docs/label-audit.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/label-audit.md). Why test labels
stay as published: [ADR 0002](decisions/0002-test-labels-never-edited.html); why train and
validation keep their noise: [ADR 0005](decisions/0005-train-and-validation-keep-label-noise.html).
:::

## Measuring it

No model judges another: every score is computed by rule. An answer is parsed into a list of calls
and compared with gold's.

- **Strict exact match** is the headline: the same calls as gold, in any order, every value equal.
- **Lenient exact** sits beside it: the same, but ignoring optional arguments written at their
  default. Gold writes some defaults out and leaves others out, and by the tool spec both are the
  same call.
- **BFCL**, the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, is a second test set of
  `{python} n(M["baselines"]["official"]["raw 0.8B"]["bfcl"]["n"])` rows whose tools come from a
  different source than xLAM's. xLAM's test asks for new values in tools the student has seen; BFCL tells tool calling apart
  from learning xLAM's tools.

Two models are always compared on the same rows. Most rows both get right or both get wrong, so
the **McNemar test** looks only at the rows where exactly one is right. For the distilled student
against its teacher on test-clean, that is `{python} bt["only_a_right"]` rows for the student and
`{python} bt["only_b_right"]` for the teacher. If the two were equally good, those rows would split
about evenly.

The project makes `{python} len(M["claims"])` such comparisons, all listed in
[results/methods.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/results/methods.md#readme-claims), and testing many raises the chance
that one looks significant by luck. So every p-value is adjusted over all of them with **Holm's
method**, and a difference is called significant only after the adjustment. Each claim below
carries its counts and adjusted p-value in small grey type.

::: {.column-margin}
The scorer and its rules: [docs/notes/details.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/notes/details.md#task); BFCL's conversion:
[docs/bfcl.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/bfcl.md); comparing methods:
[ADR 0009](decisions/0009-selection-stays-methods-compared-on-test-clean.html).
:::

## The methods

Every method starts from the same untrained 0.8B and fine-tunes it with the same LoRA adapter,
learning rate and one epoch over the training queries. The loss falls on the answer tokens only.
What changes is *who writes the text* the student trains on, and *what it is trained toward* at
each token of it (@fig-methods).

::: {#fig-methods}

```{=html}
<div class="mmap">
<div class="mhead"><span>Method</span><span>Who writes the text</span><span>What each token teaches</span></div>
<div class="mrow"><div class="mid"><span class="m m-A">A</span><small>SFT on labels</small></div><div class="src gold">xLAM's gold answer<code>"city": "Porto"</code></div><div class="sig"><svg width="34" height="26" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="12" y="2" width="10" height="22" rx="1.5" fill="var(--gold)"/></svg><span>the token gold wrote<br><small>cross-entropy · reads gold</small></span></div></div>
<div class="mrow"><div class="mid"><span class="m m-B">B</span><small>SFT on teacher answers</small></div><div class="src teacher">the teacher, once, offline<code>"city": "Porto"</code></div><div class="sig"><svg width="34" height="26" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="12" y="2" width="10" height="22" rx="1.5" fill="var(--teacher)"/></svg><span>the token the teacher wrote<br><small>cross-entropy · a hard target</small></span></div></div>
<div class="mrow"><div class="mid"><span class="m m-C">C</span><small>logit distillation</small></div><div class="src teacher">the teacher, once, offline<code>"city": "Porto"</code></div><div class="sig"><svg width="34" height="26" aria-hidden="true"><g fill="var(--teacher)"><rect x="2" y="16" width="6" height="8" rx="1"/><rect x="10" y="3" width="6" height="21" rx="1"/><rect x="18" y="12" width="6" height="12" rx="1"/><rect x="26" y="19" width="6" height="5" rx="1"/></g></svg><span>the teacher's top 20 probabilities<br><small>forward KL · a soft target</small></span></div></div>
<div class="mrow"><div class="mid"><span class="m m-D">D</span><small>on-policy distillation</small></div><div class="src student">the student, fresh every step<code>"city": "Lisbon"  ← its own guess</code></div><div class="sig"><svg width="34" height="26" aria-hidden="true"><g><rect x="1" y="6" width="7" height="14" rx="1.5" fill="#1baf7a" opacity=".35"/><rect x="9" y="6" width="7" height="14" rx="1.5" fill="#1baf7a" opacity=".2"/><rect x="17" y="6" width="7" height="14" rx="1.5" fill="#e34948" opacity=".75"/><rect x="25" y="6" width="7" height="14" rx="1.5" fill="#e34948" opacity=".3"/></g></svg><span>the teacher's grade on every token<br><small>reverse KL · on its own text</small></span></div></div>
</div>
```

Two questions sort every method: whose text the student trains on (grey: gold's, violet: the teacher's, teal: its own) and what it learns at each token of it. Everything else is shared: the untrained 0.8B, LoRA rank 16, learning rate 2e-4, 16 rows a step, one epoch.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
The shared setup, and why it is untuned:
[ADR 0006](decisions/0006-shared-training-setup.html). LoRA trains about 1.4% of the parameters
([results/sft-cost.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/results/sft-cost.md)).
:::

### Copying the teacher's answers

The simplest way to learn from a teacher is to treat its answers as labels. The 2B answers all
`{python} n(teacher["rows"])` training queries once, in `{python} f"{teacher['gpu_hours']:.1f}"`
GPU-hours. The `{python} n(teacher["variants"]["unfiltered"]["kept"])` answers that parse are kept,
and the 0.8B is fine-tuned on them with the ordinary next-token loss: that is **B**, supervised
fine-tuning on teacher outputs. **A** is the same recipe on xLAM's gold answers.

At each token, the loss is the cross-entropy of the one token written there, $-\log q(y)$: a *hard
target*. The teacher's answers are far from perfect, agreeing with gold on
`{python} pct(teacher["variants"]["unfiltered"]["lenient"])` of B's training rows under lenient exact, and the student
copies them, mistakes included.

**Result.** B reaches **`{python} story.score("B")`** on test-clean in
`{python} story.gpu_hours("B")` GPU-hours, past its teacher's `{python} story.score("raw 2B")`
[(`{python} story.claim("B", "raw 2B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}. A, with labels, reaches
`{python} story.score("A")`.

::: {.column-margin}
This is sequence-level distillation[^kim]. The runs: [#42]({{< var repo >}}/issues/42) (A),
[#46]({{< var repo >}}/issues/46) (B).
:::

[^kim]: [Kim & Rush, 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07947), *Sequence-Level Knowledge
    Distillation*.

### Soft targets: the teacher's whole distribution

A hard target says the written token is right and every other token is wrong. But at every position
the teacher has an opinion about all 248,320 tokens in its vocabulary. @fig-token shows it along
one answer, measured on both models.

::: {#fig-token}

```{=html}
<div class="widget" id="w-token">
<p class="lead">The teacher's answer to <em>"Give me the forecast for Lisbon."</em>. Pick a position where it hesitates, or one where it is sure:</p>
<div class="seg"></div>
<div class="tokline"></div>
<svg class="chart" role="img" aria-label="Teacher and student next-token probabilities"></svg>
<div class="keys"><span style="--c:var(--teacher)">teacher, 2B</span><span style="--c:var(--student)">student, 0.8B before training</span></div>
<div class="readout">
<div><div class="label">B's loss, −log q(y)</div><div class="value" data-o="hard"></div></div>
<div><div class="label">C's loss, KL(p ‖ q)</div><div class="value" data-o="soft"></div></div>
<div><div class="label">teacher's top 20 hold</div><div class="value" data-o="top"></div></div>
</div>
<p class="note"></p>
</div>
```

Hard and soft targets differ only where the teacher hesitates. The 2B's and the untrained 0.8B's
next-token probabilities along the 2B's answer to a made-up query, measured on the 3060, with each
method's loss there in nats. The 2B hesitates twice: between a list and a code fence at the first
token, and over whether to write `days` out at its default. The top 20 tokens, all C stores, hold
nearly all of its probability.
:::

A soft target trains the student toward the teacher's whole distribution $p$, with the forward KL
divergence:

$$\mathcal{L}_\text{soft} = \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_v p(v) \log \frac{p(v)}{q(v)}.$$

The hard target is the special case of a teacher that puts all its probability on one token. So the
two only differ where the teacher hesitates, as it does over whether to write `days` at all. **C**, logit
distillation, runs on B's rows and B's text exactly; the 2B scores that text once more and stores
its 20 likeliest tokens at every answer position, plus one entry for everything else. C − B then
isolates soft against hard targets.

Over all of B's training text, the teacher's written token is nearly always its first choice: it is
usually sure. That limits what C can add.

**Result.** C ties B on test-clean, `{python} story.score("C")` against `{python} story.score("B")`
[(`{python} story.claim("C", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}, at `{python} story.gpu_hours("C")`
GPU-hours. On unseen tools it leads B, `{python} story.score("C", "bfcl")` against
`{python} story.score("B", "bfcl")`, but not after Holm
[(`{python} story.claim("C", "B", "bfcl")`)]{.stat}.

::: {.column-margin}
Hinton et al. call the information in those small probabilities "dark knowledge"[^hinton]. Why the
top 20 aren't renormalised, and no temperature:
[ADR 0010](decisions/0010-method-c-stored-top-k-logit-distillation.html).
:::

[^hinton]: [Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531), *Distilling the
    Knowledge in a Neural Network*.

### On-policy: the teacher grades the student's own answers

B and C learn from text the teacher wrote: they are *off-policy*. At test time, though, the student
writes its own answers, one token after another. One early slip, a wrong function name or a missing
argument, puts it somewhere the teacher's text never went, and it never learned to recover
(@fig-prefix).

::: {#fig-prefix}

```{=html}
<div class="widget" id="w-prefix">
<div class="seg words"></div>
<div class="toks"></div>
<p class="note"></p>
</div>
```

Off-policy training only visits the teacher's prefixes. An illustration: the student closes the
list one token early, and from there on writes prefixes B and C never trained on.
:::

**D**, on-policy distillation, trains on the student's own attempts. At every step:

1. the student writes an answer to a training query, sampling at temperature 1;
2. the teacher reads that answer and gives its probability for every token, at every position;
3. the student is pushed toward the teacher's distribution, on its own text.

::: {#fig-grade}

```{=html}
<div class="widget" id="w-grade">
<p class="lead"></p>
<div class="tokrow"></div>
<p class="gold tokline"></p>
<div class="readout">
<div><div class="label">p student</div><div class="value" data-o="ps"></div></div>
<div><div class="label">p teacher</div><div class="value" data-o="pt"></div></div>
<div><div class="label">log p student − log p teacher</div><div class="value" data-o="k"></div></div>
</div>
<p class="note"></p>
</div>
```

The teacher grades every token the student wrote. Each token is shaded by
$\log q - \log p$, the student's log-probability minus the teacher's: red where the student was
surer, green where the teacher was. Measured: the untrained 0.8B's own answer to a real test-clean
row (the shortest one it gets wrong and the 2B gets right), and both models' probabilities for each of
its tokens. The student calls the right tool once, with the wrong argument name, and stops; the
heaviest penalty falls on the token that ends the call after Amazon, where the teacher expected a
second call, for Google.
:::

Unlike reinforcement learning, which gives one reward per answer, every token gets feedback. The
loss turns around too: the *reverse* KL, $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$, is large wherever the student
puts probability the teacher doesn't. It teaches the student to avoid what the teacher would never
write, rather than to cover everything the teacher considers, which is usually the better trade for
a small model. @fig-peaks shows the difference.

::: {#fig-peaks}

```{=html}
<div class="widget" id="w-peaks">
<svg class="chart" role="img" aria-label="A two-peaked teacher and a one-peaked student"></svg>
<div class="keys"><span style="--c:var(--teacher)">teacher</span><span style="--c:var(--student)">student</span></div>
<div class="controls">
<label>student's peak <input type="range" name="mu" min="0" max="20" step="0.5" value="10"></label>
<label>width <input type="range" name="sd" min="0.6" max="6" step="0.1" value="4"></label>
</div>
<div class="readout">
<div><div class="label">forward KL(p ‖ q), C's loss</div><div class="value" data-o="fwd"></div></div>
<div><div class="label">reverse KL(q ‖ p), D's loss</div><div class="value" data-o="rev"></div></div>
</div>
</div>
```

An illustration: a one-peaked student fitting a teacher torn between two answers, say `5` and `5.0`. Try a wide
student in the middle, then a narrow one on either peak: forward KL prefers the first, reverse KL the
second. For tool calls, committing to one clean answer is what exact match rewards.
:::

The price is that the teacher grades every answer during training, so D runs the student, the
teacher and a sampling engine at once on the 12 GB card.

**Result.** D ties B on test-clean, `{python} story.score("D")`
[(`{python} story.claim("D", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}, at `{python} story.gpu_hours("D")`
GPU-hours. On unseen tools it scores `{python} story.score("D", "bfcl")`, above B
[(`{python} story.claim("D", "B", "bfcl")`)]{.stat}.

::: {.column-margin}
The method: Thinking Machines' [On-Policy Distillation](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/)
and GKD[^gkd]. TRL's `DistillationTrainer` with the student sampling in vLLM:
[ADR 0008](decisions/0008-method-d-setup.html), run [#54]({{< var repo >}}/issues/54).
:::

[^gkd]: [Agarwal et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649), *On-Policy Distillation of
    Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes*.

### Filtering the teacher's answers

The teacher is often wrong, so the last experiments train only on its better answers.

- [Filtered B]{.m .m-Bf} keeps the `{python} n(teacher["variants"]["lenient"]["kept"])` answers that
  match gold. It uses labels, as a filter: it measures what the teacher's mistakes cost.
  `{python} story.score("Bf")` [(`{python} story.claim("Bf", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}.
- [Grounded B]{.m .m-Bg} keeps the `{python} n(teacher["variants"]["grounded"]["kept"])` whose every
  value is written in the query, a rule that never reads gold. `{python} story.score("Bg")`, a tie
  with B [(`{python} story.claim("Bg", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}: it gains where values are in
  the query and loses where they must be worked out.
- [Filtered C]{.m .m-Cf} is C on filtered B's rows: `{python} story.score("Cf")`.
- [B then D]{.m .m-BD} runs D's loss on top of B, as Thinking Machines do:
  `{python} story.score("B→D")`, behind B though not after Holm
  [(`{python} story.claim("B→D", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}.

::: {.column-margin}
Filtered B: [#60]({{< var repo >}}/issues/60); grounded B: [#74]({{< var repo >}}/issues/74),
[#75]({{< var repo >}}/issues/75); filtered C: [#88]({{< var repo >}}/issues/88); B then D:
[#58]({{< var repo >}}/issues/58).
:::

## Results

@fig-cost puts every method on one chart: its score on test-clean against everything it cost.

{{< include _cost_picks.qmd >}}

### The label-free methods tie, so the simplest is the headline

B, C, D and grounded B can't be separated on test-clean. Where methods tie, the cheaper is published,
and within 10% of the cheapest, the simpler pipeline. So B is the headline method. That reading of
the rule was chosen after the results were known: read literally, it names grounded B,
`{python} f"{100 * (1 - bg_cost / b_cost):.0f}%"` cheaper.

::: {.column-margin}
The rule and its reading:
[ADR 0009](decisions/0009-selection-stays-methods-compared-on-test-clean.html),
[#95]({{< var repo >}}/issues/95).
:::

### The student beats its teacher on xLAM, not on new tools

Little of B's lead over the 2B on xLAM is format: most of the 2B's answers that fail to parse are a
first call cut short, and repairing them makes almost none right. Nor is it memorisation: no
test-clean query appears verbatim in train, and B's lead is larger on rows whose tools train never offered. What it is
remains open; running the 2B on its own answers would test whether it is self-training.

::: {#fig-beats}

```{python}
example("beats-teacher")
```

Where the student beats its teacher (the shortest test-clean row where B is right and the 2B wrong).
The 2B computes the answer itself instead of calling the tool; B, trained on the 2B's own answers,
calls it. Differences from gold are marked.
:::

On BFCL's unseen tools B doesn't keep its lead: it is below the 2B, though not after Holm
[(`{python} story.claim("B", "raw 2B", "bfcl")`)]{.stat}, getting argument values wrong on tools it
never saw.

### On unseen tools, the picks overstate the differences

D's lead over B on BFCL holds at the checkpoints validation chose. Along whole runs it fades: B's
BFCL keeps rising after its pick, to `{python} pct(last["B"]["bfcl"]["exact"])` at the end of its
epoch, above D's at the same GPU-hours. With one seed, the data can't tell on-policy training from
more training. Soft targets on clean rows show the same pattern: filtered C leads filtered B at
their picks [(`{python} story.claim("Cf", "Bf", "bfcl")`)]{.stat}, and gets there sooner, but
filtered B keeps rising, and at the end of their epochs the two are not significantly different.
Faster, not better.

::: {#fig-unseen}

```{python}
example("unseen-tools")
```

On a tool neither saw in training (the shortest BFCL row where D is right and B wrong), B reads
"5,10" as one number. D, trained on its own attempts, makes the three calls. B's differences from D's
answer are marked.
:::

{{< include _bfcl.qmd >}}

Nor does on-policy pay off per GPU-hour: D's only checkpoint within B's GPU-hours (step `{python} d_budget["step"]`,
`{python} f"{d_budget['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` GPU-hours) scores
`{python} pct(d_budget["official"]["test-clean"]["exact"])` on test-clean, against B's
`{python} story.score("B")`
[(`{python} story.claim(f"D@{d_budget['step']}", "B", "test-clean")`)]{.stat}.

### Students copy the teacher's habits, and some of its mistakes

A student that agrees more with its teacher may only be getting more answers right. The test is the
teacher's own mistakes: of the `{python} bfcl_selected("B")["teacher_errors"]` BFCL rows the 2B gets
wrong, B repeats its exact answer on `{python} bfcl_selected("B")["copies_teacher_errors"]`, D on
`{python} bfcl_selected("D")["copies_teacher_errors"]` and C on
`{python} bfcl_selected("C")["copies_teacher_errors"]`. They copy some of its errors, none most.

Habits travel too. Soft targets carry the teacher's format: C fences
`{python} pct(M["formats"]["C"]["fenced"])` of its answers in a code block, as the 2B does
`{python} pct(M["formats"]["raw 2B"]["fenced"])` of the time, and B never. Labels carry gold's: on
the `{python} defaults_rows` test-clean rows where gold and a model differ only by an optional
argument written at its default, A gets `{python} pct(M["defaults"]["A"]["default_made_explicit"], 0)`
right, B `{python} pct(M["defaults"]["B"]["default_made_explicit"], 0)` and the 2B
`{python} pct(M["defaults"]["raw 2B"]["default_made_explicit"], 0)`.

::: {#fig-fenced}

```{python}
example("fenced")
```

C's answer in the teacher's code fence (the shortest test-clean row where C fences its answer). The
scorer reads the JSON inside the fence, so this one still counts as right.
:::


### The student serves faster

The point of a smaller model is serving it. In vLLM on the same card, the 0.8B answers
**`{python} serve["one_at_a_time"]` faster** than the 2B one request at a time, and serves
**`{python} serve["batched"]` cheaper** with every test-clean prompt batched: the prompts are long
and the answers short, so batching narrows the gap.

::: {.column-margin}
Settings and every run: [results/serving.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/results/serving.md)
([#63]({{< var repo >}}/issues/63)). The headline model's release: [#96]({{< var repo >}}/issues/96).
:::

## Limitations

- **One seed and one untuned setup per method.** Paired tests on the same rows make the comparisons
  fair, but a method sensitive to its learning rate may look worse than it is.
- **One small teacher.** A stronger teacher would likely lift the label-free numbers; the results
  are about this pair, on this task.
- **Single-turn tool calls only**, scored by exact match.

## Conclusion

On this task, the simplest distillation is enough. Fine-tuning a 0.8B student on a 2B teacher's
answers, with no labels at all, beats the teacher on xLAM in `{python} h["gpu_hours"]` GPU-hours,
and the more sophisticated methods, soft targets and on-policy learning, tie it. Where they differ
is on tools the student never saw, and there the differences shrink along the runs: with one seed,
more training explains them as well as the method does. Labels still buy a lot.

The open question is whether reinforcement learning, with a reward checked against gold, adds
anything on top. GRPO is the next experiment
([ADR 0007](decisions/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.html)).

Every number in this essay is computed from the repository's
[results/]({{< var repo >}}/tree/main/results) when the site builds. [Every result](results.qmd)
lists each method at its selected checkpoint, and [Decisions](decisions/index.qmd) gives every
design decision with the options it weighed.

## Reproduce it

Everything runs from the [repository]({{< var repo >}}) with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), on
one NVIDIA GPU, after accepting xLAM's terms on the Hugging Face Hub. The commands that turn the runs into this essay:

```bash
uv sync --extra inference --extra train
uv run --no-sync fc-report --methods     # results/methods.json, from the runs
uv run --no-sync fc-examples             # results/examples.json
uv run --extra train fc-probe            # data/probe/
uv run fc-figures                        # docs/figures/
uv run --group site quarto render site   # this site
```

Each run's training and eval commands, with their flags (`fc-sft`, `fc-opd`, `fc-eval`), are in its
issue, linked in the margin where the method appears.
